Allosaurus.description: A large two-legged hunter with dagger-like, saw-edged teeth, three-fingered hands and small horns above its eyes.[1]
Allosaurus.lore:
Allosaurus was one of the top hunters of North America in the Late Jurassic, tens of millions of years before Tyrannosaurus. It preyed on the plant-eating dinosaurs around it, and Stegosaurus fossils carry its bite marks.[1]

It also fed on the giant long-necked sauropods, though no one knows whether it attacked them alive or ate them after they died. It may even have torn meat from a living giant without killing it, leaving the animal to heal.[1]

Several Allosaurus have been found buried together, and some bear bite marks from their own kind. Whether they hunted in packs is unknown, but they likely competed and fought.[1] No one is sure what the small horns over its eyes were for. They may have helped Allosaurus recognize each other, served as a display for mates, or shaded its eyes from the sun.[1]

Ankylosaurus.description: A low, heavy plant-eater covered in bony armor plates, with a beaked mouth and a heavy club of bone at the end of its tail.[1]
Ankylosaurus.lore:
Ankylosaurus was an armored plant-eater from the end of the age of dinosaurs. Bony plates covered its body, and its tail ended in a heavy club.[1] It probably moved slowly most of the time, grazing on ferns, shrubs and fruit near the ground, and it needed about as much food each day as an elephant.[1]

It could not lift its tail club far, but it could swing it hard from side to side, and it probably used it to fend off big predators.[1] It ate only plants, but that does not mean it was gentle: elephants and hippos eat plants too, and both can be dangerous.[1]

No complete skeleton has ever been found, and no one knows exactly how the plates on its back were arranged.[1]

Ape.description: A large, tailless primate with long arms, strong grasping hands and a heavy jaw.[1][2]
Ape.lore:
Gorillas are the largest of the great apes. A grown male can weigh more than 200 kilograms, stand nearly two meters tall and reach almost two and a half meters from hand to hand.[1] Gorillas spend most of their time on the ground and walk on their knuckles. They are mostly quiet but can scream, bark and roar, and scientists have counted 22 different calls.[1] Older males grow a saddle of silver hair across the back.[1]

Orangutans live high in the forests of Sumatra and Borneo. They are the largest animals that live in trees, with arms much longer than their legs and hands and feet made for grasping, and they are slow and awkward on the ground.[2] They live more alone than other apes. A grown male has big cheek pads and a throat sac that makes his long call boom through the forest for a kilometer or more.[2] Some groups of orangutans make sounds that others don't, habits passed on like local customs.[2]

Archelon.description: A sea turtle more than four meters long, with large, flat front flippers, a broad, shallow shell and a hooked beak.[1]
Archelon.lore:
Archelon is the largest turtle known to have lived. It swam the warm, shallow seas of the late Cretaceous, about 80 to 74 million years ago, and the biggest one found weighed two to three tonnes.[1] Its shell was more of a frame than solid armor.[1]

It lived in the shallow sea that once cut through the middle of North America, alongside mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, sharks and huge fish.[1] Its hooked beak points to a strong bite. When attacked, it may have struck back with its flippers and beak or used its shell as a shield, though not always with success: bones of turtles like it have been found in the stomachs of mosasaurs.[1]

Like sea turtles today, Archelon probably laid its eggs on beaches.[1]

Axe Beak.description: A tall, flightless hunting bird with powerful running legs, shrunken wings and a large skull with a hooked beak.[1][2]
Axe Beak.lore:
The terror birds were giant flightless hunters, counted among the dominant predators of ancient South America. There were at least 18 kinds, from small to gigantic, and nothing alive today is quite like them.[1][2] Their wings had shrunk and their bodies were heavy, and they lived entirely on the ground.[1]

Fossil footprints about eight million years old show they were built for running. They carried their weight on one thick main toe and probably used a long, raised claw on another to pin down prey.[1] Their skulls were rigid and strong for striking downward. A terror bird likely ate mostly smaller prey, and if it took on something big, it probably attacked with repeated, well-aimed strikes of its beak, darting in and out.[2]

Baboon.description: A large monkey that lives on the ground, with a long tail and olive-gray fur. Males are nearly twice the size of females, with heavy manes and long fangs.[1]
Baboon.lore:
Baboons live in big troops that travel, feed and sleep together. Each evening the troop has to reach a safe place to sleep, up in the trees or on rocks and cliffs.[1] Young males leave the troop they were born in and have to win a place among the males of a new one.[1]

They eat almost anything: fruit, seeds, flowers, roots, insects, eggs and small animals. They can live on grass for long stretches, which lets them survive in dry country.[1]

Baboons say a lot without sound. A hard stare is a threat, made sharper by the differently colored fur around the eyes, and a wide yawn that shows off the fangs is another warning.[1] When a leopard comes near, baboons will mob it, often with the grown males leading the attack.[1]

Badger.description: A low, flat-bodied digger with short, powerful legs and a face striped black and white.[1][2]
Badger.lore:
Badgers are built for digging. The American badger tunnels through soil at speed with its powerful front legs, and it hunts by digging out gophers, ground squirrels, prairie dogs and other burrowing animals. It also eats birds, lizards, insects and even honeycomb.[1] American badgers live alone and come out mostly at night. They don't truly hibernate, but in winter they spend long spells in a deep sleep in their dens, coming out on warm days.[1]

The Eurasian badger is more sociable and lives in family groups, though each badger forages alone. Earthworms are its main food.[2] Badgers growl when threatened and wail when attacked.[2]

Badgers are known for their fierce temper, and apart from people, grown badgers have few enemies.[1][2]

Basilisk.description: A small serpent with a white mark on its head like a crown, so deadly that it withers plants and splits stones.[1]
Basilisk.lore:
Pliny the Elder wrote that the basilisk came from the province of Cyrene. It was no longer than twelve fingers, with a white spot on its head like a crown, and like the catoblepas it could kill with a look.[1] When it hissed, every other snake fled, and instead of crawling in coils it moved along with its body raised upright.[1]

It killed shrubs by touching them or even breathing on them, scorched the grass and broke stones.[1] People once believed that if a rider speared a basilisk, the poison would run up the spear and kill both the rider and his horse.[1]

Its one weakness was the weasel. A weasel thrown into a basilisk's hole, easy to find by the blighted ground around it, killed the basilisk with its smell and died itself in the struggle.[1]

Travelers' tales rarely agree about the basilisk. The creature adventurers meet is often far larger than Pliny's little serpent, and its gaze does not kill outright but slowly turns living flesh to stone.

Bat.description: A small flying mammal with wings of thin skin stretched between long finger bones, darting through the dusk after insects.[1]
Bat.lore:
Bats are the only mammals that truly fly. A bat's wing is like a hand with long fingers and thin, flexible skin stretched between them, which makes bats nimble in the air.[1] At dawn and dusk they swoop and twist after insects, catching them in flight in near darkness.[1]

When the cold drives the insects away, some bats hibernate and some fly to warmer places. In hibernation a bat's heart slows from hundreds of beats a minute to about ten, it may go minutes without a breath, and its body can cool to near freezing.[2] Some sleep this way for more than six months, waiting for the insects to return in spring.[2]

Bats are not blind. They see well, and some of the large fruit-eating bats see three times better than people.[3] Vampire bats are real: they live in Latin America and feed on the blood of cattle and other large animals, which often don't notice them.[3] For their size, bats live a long time, some up to 35 years.[3]

Black Bear.description: A shy forest bear, usually black with a pale muzzle, though some are brown, cinnamon, blond or even creamy white.[1]
Black Bear.lore:
Black bears live in thick woods and rough country across North America. Despite their size they eat mostly plants: grass in spring, berries in summer, and nuts, acorns and fruit in fall, when they put on fat for the winter.[1] Insects make up most of the meat they eat, and they take larger animals only when the chance comes.[1]

They are most active at dawn and dusk, and they spend the winter in dens, coming out in spring thin and hungry.[1] Bears that find people's food or garbage are drawn to it, and that is behind most trouble between black bears and people.[1]

Black bears are clever and curious, with a keen nose and a remarkable sense of direction.[1] They are usually timid around people, and a mother with cubs is far less likely to attack than a grizzly mother.[1]

Blood Hawk.description: A lean hawk with rust-red feathers and a hooked beak that hunts in noisy flocks.
Blood Hawk.lore:
Blood hawks nest on sea cliffs and high crags, and unlike most hawks they hunt together. A flock circles high over open ground, then drops all at once on a single animal, striking from every side until it falls.

Their name comes from the deep red of their feathers, though shepherds say it comes from what they leave behind. A flock that loses its fear of people will harass lone travelers and raid flocks of sheep and goats, and in some hill country a bounty is paid for every blood hawk killed.

Falconers have tried to train them, with little success. A blood hawk will hunt for a handler, but only alongside others of its kind.

Boar.description: A wild pig with a thick, coarse coat, often with a ridge of long bristles down its back, and a long snout made for rooting.[1]
Boar.lore:
Wild boars live in groups called sounders, made up of several sows and their young. Grown males mostly live alone and join the groups to mate.[1] They eat mostly plants, such as nuts, fruit, roots and crops, but also eggs, worms, insects, small rodents and carrion, and now and then a lamb or calf.[1]

They forage mostly in the evening and at night. On hot days they lie in the shade and wallow in water and mud, which cools them and keeps insects off.[1] Their sense of smell is keen. They growl when angry and squeal when excited.[1]

Piglets are born with striped coats that hide them in the undergrowth.[1] Boars can do great damage to farmland, and people are their main hunters.[1]

Brown Bear.description: A huge bear with fur from cream to nearly black. In the Rocky Mountains, white-tipped hairs give it a grizzled look, which is where the grizzly bear gets its name.[1]
Brown Bear.lore:
Brown bears are among the largest meat-eaters on land. Standing on its hind legs, a big one towers about two and a half meters tall, and a brown bear is strong enough to kill a cow with a single blow and fast enough to outrun a horse.[1]

They eat almost anything: grass, roots, berries, nuts, insects and fungi, ground squirrels and marmots dug out of their burrows, and in some places moose, elk, mountain sheep and spawning salmon.[1] In autumn a bear may travel hundreds of kilometers to reach a salmon stream or a good berry crop.[1]

Brown bears usually live alone and avoid people. They rarely attack unless surprised up close, guarding cubs or busy with food, but their temper is hard to predict.[1] Their nose is excellent, able to follow the smell of a rotting carcass for more than three kilometers, though their eyesight is poor.[1]

Camel.description: A tall desert animal with a long curved neck, a fatty hump, thick lips for eating thorny plants and broad, padded feet for walking on sand.[1]
Camel.lore:
The dromedary, the one-humped camel, is built for the desert. Its hump is a store of fat for hard times, and it shrinks and leans to one side when the camel goes hungry.[1] A double row of eyelashes keeps out blowing sand, and the camel saves water in many ways, including not sweating as the day heats up.[1]

Camels eat thorny plants, dry grass, saltbush and almost anything else that grows in the desert, taking only a few leaves from each plant as they go. They spend long hours grazing and as long again chewing the cud.[1]

They live in small family groups of a male and several females with their young.[1] They are mostly calm, but rutting males fight. When camels quarrel, they shove each other, snap without biting, and sometimes throw up their cud when hurt or excited.[1] People use them to carry loads and for milk, meat, wool and leather, and camels have made it possible to live in some of the driest lands.[1]

Cat.description: A small, agile hunter with soft fur, sharp claws, keen ears and long whiskers.[1]
Cat.lore:
Cats probably descend from African wild cats or Asian desert cats, and they live almost wherever people do.[1] There are more than a hundred breeds, but they all share much the same shape and size.[1]

A cat marks its ground by rubbing against things, scratching with its claws and spraying, each of which leaves scent behind.[1] It purrs when content, meows, and growls, hisses or spits when upset. Its ears can swivel to face forward, back or anywhere between.[1]

Cats are meat-eaters, and like all cats they kill with a bite to the back of the neck.[1] Cats gone wild hunt mice and birds, and in some places they have badly reduced the number of wild birds.[1]

Centaur.description: A creature with the head, arms and chest of a man joined to the body of a horse.[1]
Centaur.lore:
The centaurs were wild, cloud-born creatures, men above and horses below.[1] Ovid tells of the wedding of Pirithous, king of the Lapiths, who invited the centaurs to his feast. Eurytus, the most savage of them, was inflamed by wine and by the sight of the bride, and he seized her by the hair, while the other centaurs grabbed whatever women they could. The feast became a battle between the centaurs and the Lapiths, and many died on both sides.[1]

Not every centaur was a brute. Ovid describes young Cyllarus, as handsome as a statue in his human half, with a golden beard and hair to his shoulders, and a horse's body as fine as the man above it, blacker than pitch.[1]

Chimera.description: A fire-breathing monster with three heads: a lion's in front, a goat's in the middle and a serpent's behind.[1]
Chimera.lore:
The Chimera was born of Echidna, the mother of monsters. It was huge, fast and strong, a creature to be feared, and it breathed out a blast of raging fire.[1]

The hero Bellerophon killed it with the help of the winged horse Pegasus, who carried him through the air as swiftly as the wind.[1]

sources.title: Theogony and Works and Days, in Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica

Cloud Giant.description: An enormous giant who lives in a great house above the clouds, among treasures such as a hen that lays golden eggs.[1]
Cloud Giant.lore:
When Jack climbed the magic beanstalk all the way to the sky, he found a long road and, at its end, a great tall house. A huge woman stood on the doorstep. Her husband, she warned him, was an ogre, and he liked nothing better than boys broiled on toast.[1] The giant shook the house with his footsteps. He came home with calves hanging from his belt, sniffed the air and roared that he smelled the blood of an Englishman.[1]

The giant was rich. After breakfast he counted his bags of gold, and he kept a hen that laid a golden egg whenever he told it to, and a golden harp that sang him to sleep. Jack stole all three. The harp cried out for its master, and the giant chased Jack down the beanstalk until Jack chopped it through and the giant fell and broke his head.[1]

Other tales tell of cloud giants who float through the air, call up banks of fog and strike with the force of thunder.

Constrictor Snake.description: A heavy-bodied snake with no venom that kills by wrapping its prey in its coils and squeezing.[1]
Constrictor Snake.lore:
The boa constrictor is famous for its size, though other snakes grow far larger, and most are two to three meters long.[1] It hunts mostly from ambush, often hanging from a branch and striking fast at whatever passes below. It eats mainly small mammals, including bats, and birds, but it will take any animal it can catch and fit in its mouth.[1]

A boa has no venom. It wraps its prey in its coils and squeezes until the animal can no longer breathe.[1] Boas live alone and are active at night or at dusk, though they bask in the sun when it is cool.[1] When a boa is about to shed its skin, its eyes turn cloudy and it often stays still until the old skin comes off.[1] Threatened, it bites.[1]

Crab.description: A hard-shelled crustacean that grows by shedding its shell and growing a new one.[1]
Crab.lore:
The blue crab of the Atlantic coast has a Latin name that means "beautiful savory swimmer".[1] It eats almost anything: clams, oysters, mussels, smaller crustaceans, fresh dead fish, rotting plants and animals, and smaller blue crabs.[1] Large fish, herons and sea turtles hunt it in turn.[1]

A crab grows by molting: it sheds its hard shell, and for a short time after it is soft.[1] A male guards his mate by cradling her for days, and he stays with her after mating until her new shell hardens. A female can carry more than three million eggs.[1]

Crocodile.description: A long, armored reptile with powerful jaws that lies almost hidden in the water until it lunges.[1]
Crocodile.lore:
Crocodiles hunt from ambush. The saltwater crocodile, the largest reptile alive, waits in the water with only its nostrils, eyes and part of its back showing, then lunges at prey that comes close. It usually kills with one snap of its jaws and drags its catch under the water.[1]

A young crocodile eats insects, frogs, crabs and small fish. A grown one takes turtles, snakes, birds, wild boar, monkeys and even buffalo.[1] Big males reach six or seven meters long, while females rarely pass three.[1]

The saltwater crocodile is counted among the cleverest reptiles. It communicates with barks, hisses and coughs, and newborns call out as they hatch.[1] A female buries 40 to 60 eggs in a mound of plants and mud.[1] Males guard stretches of river fiercely and drive rivals out to sea.[1]

Death Dog.lore:
Orthus was the hound of Geryon, the three-bodied giant of the island of Erythia, and the first child Echidna bore to the monster Typhaon.[1] He had two heads.[2]

He kept watch over Geryon's red cattle until Heracles came to take them as his tenth labor. The dog rushed at the hero, and Heracles struck it dead with his club.[2]

Deer.description: A slender, quick deer with a reddish summer coat that turns grayer in winter. Its white tail flashes as it bounds away.[1]
Deer.lore:
The white-tailed deer is one of the shyest deer. When startled it bounds off through tangled woods at nearly 50 kilometers an hour, waving its white tail from side to side.[1] It swims well too, and takes to streams and lakes to escape predators or biting insects.[1]

Deer feed mainly around dawn and dusk, on buds, twigs, shrubs and whatever else grows where they live, from maple and birch in eastern forests to cactus in the desert.[1] They keep to small home ranges and wear paths by using the same routes again and again.[1]

They see and hear well but trust their noses most to warn them of danger.[1] They talk with grunts, wheezes and bleats, and a disturbed deer gives a sharp whistle or snort. Glands on their feet and legs leave scent for other deer to read.[1] Wolves, mountain lions, bears, jaguars, coyotes and people all hunt them.[1]

Dire Wolf.description: A wolf heavier and more muscular than any wolf alive today, with a big head, powerful jaws and large, strong teeth.[1][2]
Dire Wolf.lore:
Dire wolves hunted across the Americas during the last ice age, from Alaska down into South America, in grasslands, open woods and wetlands alike. Their Latin name means "terrible wolf".[1] They stood about as tall as a gray wolf but were around a quarter heavier, with much larger heads and a stronger bite.[2]

They probably hunted in packs, and thousands of their fossils have been dug from the tar pits of Rancho La Brea in Los Angeles.[1] Horses were their main prey, along with bison, giant ground sloths and camels.[1][2] Many of their teeth are broken, a sign that they fought over carcasses and chewed bone, and when food ran short they may have stolen kills from saber-toothed cats.[1][2]

Despite the name, dire wolves were not close kin to gray wolves. The two lines split millions of years ago and only came to look alike because they lived alike.[1][2] When the great ice age animals died out, dire wolves struggled to compete with gray wolves for smaller prey, and they disappeared about 10,000 years ago.[1][2]

Draft Horse.description: A strong, deep-chested working horse bred to pull wagons, plows and farm machines.[1][2][3]
Draft Horse.lore:
Before tractors, farms and ranches ran on the strength of horses. They pulled plows and carriages, and their manure fed the fields.[3] At Grant-Kohrs Ranch in Montana, Belgian draft horses were bred from purebred bloodlines from the late 1920s, and Belgian and Percheron teams still pull threshing equipment and hay wagons there.[1]

Haying was one of their great tasks. With horse-drawn mowers and rakes, prairie grass was cut, dried, raked and stacked, so there would be enough hay to feed the animals through the winter.[2]

Dryad.description: A nymph of the woods who dances with her sisters in the sacred groves, her life bound to a tree.[1]
Dryad.lore:
Dryads are the nymphs of the woods. In Ovid's tale, the Dryads used to dance hand in hand around a vast, ancient oak in a grove sacred to the goddess Ceres, its trunk hung with garlands and with tokens of prayers that had been answered.[1]

The impious Erysichthon ordered the oak cut down. When his servants hesitated, he took the axe himself and killed a man who tried to stop him. As the blade bit, the oak shuddered and groaned, blood ran from the bark, and a voice inside cried that a nymph dear to Ceres was dying within it, and that his punishment was near.[1]

The other Dryads went to Ceres in mourning, and the goddess sent Famine to fill Erysichthon with a hunger that nothing could satisfy.[1] Some nymphs, the hamadryads, were said to live and die with their trees.[1]

Eagle.description: A huge, dark brown bird of prey with long, broad wings and golden feathers on the back of its head and neck.[1]
Eagle.lore:
The golden eagle is the largest bird of prey in North America, with wings more than two meters across.[1] It hunts rabbits, hares, ground squirrels and marmots, and sometimes much larger prey: hoofed animals, coyotes, badgers, and geese and cranes taken in the air.[1] A pair often hunts together, one chasing the prey until it tires while the other swoops in for the kill.[1]

It usually flies at around 50 kilometers an hour but can pass 300 in a dive.[1] Golden eagles are mostly silent. Instead of calling, they defend their territory with a rolling, swooping flight along its edge.[1] Some live in one place all year, while those of the far north fly south for the winter.[1]

Elephant.description: The largest animal on land, with thick gray skin, great flapping ears, ivory tusks and a long trunk strong enough to lift heavy loads.[1]
Elephant.lore:
Elephants are the largest animals living on land.[1] Their trunk is nose and upper lip joined into one, with no bone in it, and they use it to smell, touch, drink, feed, dust themselves, lift, push and fight.[1] Their tusks are long front teeth of ivory, used to dig for water and roots, strip bark, rescue calves and fight.[1]

Elephants live in herds of related females and their young. Among African elephants a matriarch leads the herd, while Asian herds have no single leader.[1] Young males leave the herd between eight and thirteen years old and spend more and more time alone as they age.[1] They eat leaves, fruit, grass, bark and roots, and they will push over a whole tree to get at its bark or roots.[2]

Elephants call to each other with rumbles too low for people to hear, which other elephants can pick up more than three kilometers away.[1] They are clever and learn much of what they do rather than being born knowing it.[1] Grown elephants have no enemies except people.[1]

Elk.description: One of the largest deer, with a dark brown mane, a light brown body and a pale rump. Bulls carry wide antlers of solid bone.[1]
Elk.lore:
Elk live in herds that can grow to a few hundred, mostly cows, calves and young bulls. Older bulls keep to themselves or travel in small groups until the fall.[1] Herds move with the seasons, climbing to high meadows in summer and coming down to lower valleys for the winter.[1]

A bull grows new antlers every spring, as fast as two and a half centimeters a day, and drops them every winter. A grown bull's antlers can weigh 18 kilograms.[1]

In autumn, bulls compete for cows. They fight less than they show off, displaying their antlers, necks and bodies and giving off a strong, musky smell.[1] Above all they bugle: a deep call that climbs to a high squeal and ends in grunts, echoing through the autumn nights to warn off rivals.[1] In early summer, cows are fiercely protective of their spotted calves.[1]

Erinyes.description: One of the dread goddesses of vengeance, born from the blood of the first sky god.[1][2]
Erinyes.lore:
When Cronus wounded his father, the Sky, the drops of blood fell on the Earth, and from them she bore the Erinyes, the Furies, along with the Giants.[1] Apollodorus names three of them: Alecto, Tisiphone and Megaera.[2] Hesiod warns of the fifth day of the month, when the Erinyes attended the birth of Oath, whom Strife bore to trouble those who break their word.[1]

In other tales the Erinyes serve in the ranks of the hells, armored warriors who wield withering swords and magic ropes to bind their prey.

Ettin.description: A terrible giant with more than one head, who asks riddles of the travelers it catches.[1]
Ettin.lore:
In the Scottish tale of the Red Ettin, the Ettin was a monster with three heads who spared no one he caught. He had stolen the daughter of the king of Scotland, and dreadful two-headed beasts with four horns on each head roamed the land near his castle.[1] When he came home, he sniffed out any human hiding there. Each of his heads asked a riddle, and anyone who could not answer all three was struck with a mallet and turned into a pillar of stone.[1]

A young man who had been kind to a fairy learned the answers from her. The thing without an end is a bowl. The smaller it is, the more dangerous: a bridge. The dead carry the living when a ship sails with people on board. With his power broken, the Ettin lost all three heads to the young man's axe. The young man freed the king's daughter and the other women the Ettin had locked away, and touched the stone pillar with a magic wand to bring his brother back to life.[1]

Other tales give the ettin two heads rather than three, with a battleaxe in one hand and a morningstar in the other. With two heads keeping watch, it is very hard to catch off guard.

Fire Giant.description: A towering giant of the burning south, who carries a sword of flame and will one day set the whole world on fire.[1]
Fire Giant.lore:
Far to the south lies Muspelheim, a land so hot and bright that no one born elsewhere can bear it. The giant Surt stands guard at its border with a flaming sword in his hand.[1]

At the end of the world, the sky will split open and the sons of Muspel will ride out through the gap, with Surt at their head and fire before and behind him. His sword shines brighter than the sun. As they ride over the rainbow bridge, it breaks apart beneath them.[1]

In the last battle Surt fights the god Frey, who falls because he gave his own good sword away long before. When the gods and their enemies have destroyed each other, Surt flings fire over the earth and burns the whole world.[1]

Flying Snake.description: A slender tree snake that launches itself from high branches and glides through the air with its body flattened.[1][2]
Flying Snake.lore:
Flying snakes live in the forests of South and Southeast Asia. They don't truly fly, but they glide.[2] The paradise tree snake flings itself from the treetops, flattens and stiffens its body into an S-shape, and ripples as it falls to stay steady.[1][2]

By twisting its body it can turn in midair and steer toward a landing. Glides of more than 20 meters have been measured, and some snakes have been reported landing on branches about a hundred meters away.[1][2]

Frog.description: A big green or brown frog with long, fully webbed hind feet, a wide mouth and large round eardrums behind its eyes.[1]
Frog.lore:
Bullfrogs are the largest true frogs in North America.[1] They hunt by sitting still and waiting, sometimes for a long time, until something comes close, then snatch it with a flick of the tongue.[1] They eat almost anything they can swallow: insects, worms, crayfish, snakes, other frogs and tadpoles, and on rare occasions even bats. They will eat their own kind without hesitation.[1]

A male's deep "jug-o-rum" can be heard more than a kilometer away.[1] When the weather turns cold, a bullfrog buries itself in the mud and hibernates in a small hollow until spring.[1] Herons, turtles, water snakes, raccoons and kingfishers all hunt bullfrogs, and people catch them for frog legs.[1]

Frost Giant.description: An enormous giant of ice and cold, of the race born from the first giant, who waits for the end of the world to make war on the gods.[1]
Frost Giant.lore:
Before the world was made, rime from the icy north met the heat of the south, and the melting drops became Ymir, the first giant. While he slept, a man and a woman grew from under his arm, and from them came the frost giants. Ymir was wicked, and so was the whole race that came from him.[1]

Odin and his brothers killed Ymir. So much blood poured from him that it drowned the whole race of frost giants except one, Bergelmer, who escaped in a boat with his wife and began the race again. The gods made the earth from Ymir's flesh, the sea from his blood, the rocks from his bones and the sky from his skull.[1]

The frost giants never forgave it. They would climb into heaven if the fire burning on the rainbow bridge did not keep them back.[1] At the end of the world, the giant Hrym will lead all the frost giants to the last battle against the gods.[1]

sources.title: The Younger Edda, Also Called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda

Giant Ape.description: A huge, heavy ape about three meters tall, with massive jaws and great grinding teeth.[1]
Giant Ape.lore:
Gigantopithecus was the largest primate that ever lived, standing about three meters tall and weighing 200 to 300 kilograms.[1] It lived in the forests of southern China for some two million years, and almost everything known about it comes from four jawbones and nearly two thousand teeth found in caves.[1] Its huge teeth suggest it ate plants, chewing tough, fibrous food and plenty of fruit.[1]

It thrived while the land was a mix of forest and grass. Between about 295,000 and 215,000 years ago the seasons grew harsher and the forests thinned out. An ancient orangutan living alongside it changed its diet and survived, but Gigantopithecus could not adapt, and its numbers dwindled until it died out.[1]

sources.title: The demise of the giant ape Gigantopithecus blacki
sources.author: Yingqi Zhang and others (2024)

Giant Badger.description: A badger the size of a bear, low and broad, with a striped face and long claws that can dig through packed earth.
Giant Badger.lore:
Giant badgers dig. A single one can carve out a burrow large enough for a person to walk upright, with side chambers for sleeping and storing food, and an old burrow may be used for generations until the hillside above it is riddled with tunnels.

They hunt by night, digging other burrowing animals out of the ground, and when food is scarce they break into cellars and grain pits. Farmers know them by the fresh mounds of earth they leave behind.

A giant badger would rather dig away than fight, but it does not back down when cornered. Its temper is famous, and it keeps fighting long after wiser animals would have fled.

Giant Bat.description: A huge bat with a fox-like face, long pointed ears and wings spanning a meter and a half.[1]
Giant Bat.lore:
The large flying fox is one of the biggest bats in the world.[1] Flying foxes live in noisy colonies that can number in the thousands, roosting by day in tall trees above the forest, and their claws strip the bark and leaves from roost trees they use for years.[1]

At sunset they fly out to feed, some traveling 50 kilometers in a night, and they return at dawn.[1] Unlike most bats, they find their way by sight rather than by echolocation.[1] They eat fruit, flowers and nectar, slicing into fruit with their teeth and lapping up juice and nectar with long tongues, and a flying fox can eat half its own weight in fruit in a day.[1] They are silent in flight but loud while feeding and when they return to the roost.[1]

sources.title: Pteropus vampyrus (large flying fox)
sources.author: Kelsie Norton

Giant Boar.description: A massive, bristly, slate-gray hog with a broad head, big pointed ears and tusks that flare outward.[1]
Giant Boar.lore:
The giant forest hog stands about a meter tall and nearly two meters long.[1] It keeps to dense thickets and forest near water and comes out into clearings and grassland to feed, mostly at night. It lives in groups of six to fourteen, led by a male.[1]

Unlike other pigs, it can't root with its snout. It digs with its tusks for roots and minerals and otherwise grazes on grass and plants, eating carrion or eggs now and then.[1] It is shy and seldom seen, and much about it is still unknown.[1]

sources.title: Hylochoerus meinertzhageni (giant forest hog)
sources.author: Barbara Lundrigan
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Centipede.description: A long, flat, many-legged hunter with spiny back legs and a pair of venomous fangs in front.[1]
Giant Centipede.lore:
Giant centipedes live in the tropical forests of northern South America, hiding under rocks and in damp soil because they dry out easily.[1] They are fierce hunters. Their front legs are fangs that carry venom, and they eat crickets, worms, snails and roaches, and even lizards, toads and mice.[1]

Each segment of the body carries one pair of legs, and the spiny rear legs help fend off attackers.[1] A mother guards her eggs and stays with her young until they can feed themselves.[1]

sources.title: Scolopendra gigantea (Amazonian giant centipede)
sources.author: Catherine Meshew
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Constrictor Snake.description: An immense olive-green snake with dark oval spots, up to nine meters long and thirty centimeters thick.[1]
Giant Constrictor Snake.lore:
The green anaconda is one of the largest snakes in the world. Females are far bigger than males and can weigh 250 kilograms.[1] It lives in the rivers, streams and flooded grasslands of northern South America and spends most of its time in the water, with its eyes and nose on top of its head so it can see and breathe while swimming.[1]

It has no venom. It seizes prey in its jaws and squeezes it in its coils until it can't breathe, then swallows it whole.[1] Young anacondas eat fish, birds and small mammals, while adults take deer, capybara, caimans and large birds, and a female will sometimes eat a male.[1] It finds prey by tasting the air with its tongue, by feeling vibrations, and with heat-sensing pits on its upper lip.[1]

sources.title: Green anaconda
sources.publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute

Giant Crab.description: A crab with a pear-shaped shell and spindly legs so long that a big one measures nearly four meters from claw tip to claw tip.[1]
Giant Crab.lore:
The Japanese spider crab is the largest arthropod alive. Its shell is only about 37 centimeters long, but its legs give it a reach of nearly four meters.[1] It lives on the sandy, rocky sea floor, usually 150 to 300 meters down, and moves into shallower water to spawn.[1]

It is a slow, calm scavenger that cannot swim. It crawls along the bottom picking at dead and rotting plants and animals, eats some kelp, and now and then catches small, slow animals.[1] Sailors once told tales of these crabs dragging men under the water to eat them.[1] Young spider crabs disguise themselves with sponges and seaweed, but adults are too big to need it.[1]

sources.title: Macrocheira kaempferi (Japanese spider crab)
sources.author: William Riebel

Giant Crocodile.description: A crocodile twelve to fifteen meters long, with jaws lined with teeth as long as a hand.[1]
Giant Crocodile.lore:
Deinosuchus, the "super-croc", was among the largest crocodiles ever known. Its fossils have been found in Big Bend National Park in Texas, where it lived in swamps in the age of dinosaurs.[1]

It probably hunted the way crocodiles do today, lying submerged near the shore and seizing large dinosaurs as they fed among the plants.[1] Dinosaur bones from the same rocks are heavily damaged and covered in its bite marks.[1]

sources.title: "Super-Croc"
sources.publisher: U.S. National Park Service (Big Bend National Park)

Giant Eagle.description: An eagle of enormous size with huge talons, strong enough to bring down prey many times its own weight.[1]
Giant Eagle.lore:
Haast's eagle was the largest eagle known. It weighed about 15 kilograms and lived in New Zealand until around 700 years ago.[1] It hunted moa, giant flightless birds that could stand four meters tall and weigh hundreds of kilograms, prey no other bird of prey has had to face.[1]

It struck a moa down with its huge talons, then killed it with its beak. The prey was far too heavy to carry off, so the eagle ate it where it fell, feeding on its insides like a vulture.[1] Its head was vulture-like while its feet were those of an eagle, a mix that puzzled scientists for centuries, and it has been called "the flying tiger".[1]

sources.title: The world's largest eagle hunted unlike any other bird of prey
sources.author: James Ashworth

Giant Elk.description: A deer as tall as a doorway at the shoulder, with a hump over its shoulders and vast antlers up to three and a half meters across.[1]
Giant Elk.lore:
The giant deer, often called the Irish elk, lived across Europe for hundreds of thousands of years and died out about 8,000 years ago, probably as the climate changed.[1] People painted it on cave walls in what is now southern France more than 20,000 years ago.[1] Despite its name it was not an elk, and its closest living relative is the fallow deer.[1]

The males' antlers could reach three and a half meters across. They were hard to carry and took a great deal of food to grow, and each spring the males shed them and grew a new pair over the summer.[1] Thick skulls, sturdy necks and a muscular hump over the shoulders helped them bear the weight.[1]

The antlers were for winning mates. In autumn the males likely gathered to roar, parade side by side and lock antlers, while the females looked on and chose.[1]

sources.title: The Irish elk: when and why did this giant deer go extinct and what did it look like?
sources.author: Beth Askham and Lisa Hendry

Giant Fire Beetle.description: A large beetle that glows with a steady yellowish-green light from patches on its body.[1]
Giant Fire Beetle.lore:
Some click beetles make their own light, as fireflies do. Depending on the kind, their glowing organs sit on the back just behind the head, on the belly, or in both places.[1] The Caribbean click beetle Ignelater luminosus has lanterns in both places, and its light comes from almost the same chemistry that fireflies use. Even so, click beetles and fireflies seem to have learned to glow separately.[2]

A glowing click beetle discovered in the forests of Yunnan, China, in 2017 gives off a steady yellowish-green light from its belly while it flies, raising its abdomen to show the glow. Researchers found it by searching the dark forest for flashes at night.[1]

Giant Frog.description: A huge, flat, greenish-brown frog with webbed feet and eyes almost as wide as a coin.[1]
Giant Frog.lore:
The goliath frog is the largest frog on Earth, more than 30 centimeters long and over three kilograms.[1] It lives by fast rivers and waterfalls in warm, wet rainforest.[1]

It hunts at night along the rivers, eating insects, crabs, fish, snails, small mammals and other frogs.[1] Young goliath frogs spend most of their time underwater, while older ones bask on rocks, where their mottled skin blends with the wet moss.[1] Its tadpoles eat only one water plant, which grows near waterfalls and streams.[1]

sources.title: Conraua goliath (goliath frog)
sources.author: Sunaina Khandelwal
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Goat.description: A goat as big as a horse, with thick shaggy hair, a long beard and heavy curling horns.
Giant Goat.lore:
Giant goats live on high, rocky slopes where little else can climb. They leap across gaps and balance on ledges no wider than a hand, grazing on the tough grasses and shrubs that grow between the stones.

Each herd follows an old female who knows the safe paths and the hidden springs. In autumn the males fight for the herd, rearing up and crashing their horns together with a crack that echoes across the valleys.

Mountain folk tame them as mounts and pack animals for paths that no horse could take. A giant goat does not forget rough handling, though, and an unkind rider tends to end up in a snowbank.

Giant Hyena.description: A massive, short-faced hyena weighing more than a hundred kilograms, with jaws made for cracking bones.[2]
Giant Hyena.lore:
Pachycrocuta, the giant short-faced hyena, roamed Europe more than a million years ago.[1][2] It lived off the kills of saber-toothed cats and other big hunters, either scavenging what they left or stealing their prey outright.[1]

The remains of one of its dens, at Venta Micena in Spain, show how it fed. Each hyena seems to have foraged alone. It pulled carcasses apart, carried the marrow-rich leg bones back to its den and cracked them open there.[2] Early humans may have competed with giant hyenas for the same carcasses.[1]

When the saber-toothed cats it depended on died out in Europe, the giant hyena seems to have disappeared with them.[1]

sources.title: Computer simulation of scavenging by hominins and giant hyenas in the late Early Pleistocene
sources.author: Jesús Rodríguez and others (2023)

sources.title: Déjà vu: a reappraisal of the taphonomy of quarry VM4 of the Early Pleistocene site of Venta Micena (Baza Basin, SE Spain)
sources.author: Paul Palmqvist and others (2022)

Giant Lizard.description: A huge, stone-colored lizard with a long tail, sturdy legs, a strong neck and a yellow forked tongue.[1]
Giant Lizard.lore:
The Komodo dragon is the largest lizard alive. Most weigh about 70 kilograms, and the biggest on record was more than three meters long.[1] It lives only on a few Indonesian islands, including Komodo and Flores.[1]

It eats almost any meat, from rodents to water buffalo, and deer are its favorite. It hunts by stealth, waiting for hours beside a game trail before it attacks.[1] Its bite is venomous, and venom and bacteria in its saliva kill bitten prey within a few days.[1] Its jaws open unusually wide and its stomach stretches, so a grown dragon can eat up to 80 percent of its own weight in one meal.[1]

sources.title: Komodo dragon
sources.publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute

Giant Octopus.description: An octopus grown far past natural size that hides by changing the color and texture of its skin, then seizes prey with eight suckered arms.[1]
Giant Octopus.lore:
The giant octopus spends most of its life alone in a den under a boulder or in a crack in the rock, sometimes staying hidden for weeks. It comes out only to hunt, to mate or to flee.[1] It carries its catch home to eat, and the broken shells of clams and crabs pile up outside the entrance.[1]

It hunts by sight, stalking or chasing its prey or lying in wait, and it can change the color and even the texture of its skin to blend in.[1] Every sucker on its arms can feel and taste what it touches.[1] When attacked, it fights back with its arms, then shoots away and leaves a cloud of ink behind.[1]

It is a clever animal. It finds its way by landmarks, uses objects as tools and learns by watching, and octopuses kept in captivity are known for escaping their tanks.[1] A mother guards her eggs in the den and does not leave them even to eat. She dies before they hatch or soon after.[1]

sources.title: Enteroctopus dofleini (giant Pacific octopus)
sources.author: Colleen Hartis
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Owl.description: The largest owl in the world, brown and tawny with prominent ear tufts and huge orange eyes.[1]
Giant Owl.lore:
The Eurasian eagle-owl is the largest owl alive.[1] It lives in forests, deserts, mountains and farmland, and it prefers rocky country, especially for nesting.[1] It hunts mostly at night, taking prey in the air or on the ground, and its wings make almost no sound, so its prey rarely knows it is coming.[1]

It eats almost anything it can catch: rats, mice, voles and beetles, crows and ducks, other owls, and even foxes and young deer.[1] Eagle-owls live alone and defend their territories fiercely.[1] They are heard far more often than seen, and an eagle-owl can judge a rival's size and distance from the strength of its call.[1]

sources.title: Bubo bubo (Eurasian eagle-owl)
sources.author: Jessie Cantrell
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Rat.description: A rat almost a meter long from nose to tail tip, with coarse brown fur, dark rings around its eyes and cheek pouches that stretch to hold great loads of food.[1]
Giant Rat.lore:
The Gambian pouched rat is one of the giant pouched rats of Africa.[1] It can't bear the heat of the day, so it sleeps in tunnels or hollow trees and comes out at night to forage.[1]

It is a hoarder. It stuffs its cheek pouches with as much food as they will hold, from fruit, nuts and roots to termites and snails, and carries it home.[1] It screeches to communicate, and it sometimes moves into towns, where it can become a pest.[1]

sources.title: Cricetomys gambianus (Gambian pouched rat)
sources.author: Michael S. Joo
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Scorpion.description: A big, glossy black scorpion with two huge pincers and a long tail ending in a stinger.[1]
Giant Scorpion.lore:
The emperor scorpion is one of the largest scorpions in the world, about 20 centimeters long.[1] It lives in hot, humid forests, burrowing under leaf litter, along stream banks and even in termite mounds, and termites are its main food.[1] It comes out only after dark. Its eyesight is very poor, so it senses its surroundings and its prey through hairs on its body and comb-like organs underneath.[1]

A grown emperor scorpion rarely stings its prey. It tears it apart with its powerful pincers instead, and only the young rely on their stings.[1] For all its fierce looks it is timid, and it would rather flee than fight unless it is cornered.[1]

sources.title: Pandinus imperator (emperor scorpion)
sources.author: Cheryl Li and Sahil Parikh
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Seahorse.description: The largest seahorse, up to 35 centimeters long, with a long, toothless snout, eyes that move independently and a curling tail it uses to hold on.[1]
Giant Seahorse.lore:
The pot-bellied seahorse is the largest seahorse known.[1] It lives in shallow coastal waters, in reefs, bays, harbors and rock pools, anchoring itself to plants, coral or sponges with its curling tail.[1] It is most active at dusk and at night, feeding on tiny shrimp and other small crustaceans.[1]

The male carries the young in a pouch on his belly. He gives birth at night, most often under a full moon.[1]

sources.title: Hippocampus abdominalis (pot-bellied seahorse)
sources.author: Natalie May
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Shark.description: A shark of colossal size, far bigger than any shark alive, with serrated teeth as long as a hand.[1]
Giant Shark.lore:
Megalodon, whose name means "large tooth", was the largest shark that ever lived and one of the largest fish of all time. It ruled the seas for nearly 20 million years and died out about 3.6 million years ago.[1] A recent study suggests it may have grown to more than 24 meters long, about four times the length of the biggest great white, and weighed up to 94 tonnes.[1]

It ate meat: most likely whales, large fish and other sharks. Fossil whale bones carry the cut marks of its teeth, and some still hold the tips of teeth that snapped off as it fed.[1] Its jaws may have opened nearly three and a half meters wide, enough to swallow two grown people side by side.[1]

Its teeth reach nearly 18 centimeters long, more than three times the size of a great white's. Megalodon was long pictured as a giant great white, but it may have been a much slimmer shark.[1]

sources.title: Megalodon: The truth about the largest shark that ever lived
sources.author: Josh Davis

Giant Spider.description: A huge, hairy, brown-black spider with legs spanning nearly 30 centimeters and fangs it strikes downward to stab its prey.[1][2]
Giant Spider.lore:
The Goliath bird-eating tarantula is the heaviest spider in the world, and females can weigh about 100 grams.[2] It lives in silk-lined burrows in the rainforests of northern South America.[1] Despite its name it rarely eats birds. It feeds mostly on insects, with frogs, mice and other small animals now and then.[1][2] Its eyesight is poor, so it senses prey through vibrations picked up by sensitive hairs on its legs.[2]

Threatened, it rubs its hairs together to make a hiss that can be heard about five meters away, rears up to show its fangs, and flicks stinging hairs from its abdomen at its attacker.[1][2]

sources.title: Goliath bird-eating tarantula
sources.publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute

Giant Toad.description: A big, warty, olive-brown toad with huge poison glands behind its eyes and a bony ridge over its snout.[1]
Giant Toad.lore:
The cane toad is a big tropical toad that hunts at night, eating ants, beetles and other insects along with snails, crabs, plants and even pet food left outside.[1] When threatened it oozes a thick white poison from the glands on its back, which can sicken or kill an animal that bites it.[1]

People carried the cane toad around the world in the hope that it would eat pests in sugar cane fields, and it is now the most widely introduced amphibian of all. It did not control the pests and has become a pest itself, eating and outcompeting native frogs and poisoning the animals that try to eat it.[1]

sources.title: Rhinella marina (cane toad)
sources.author: Ryan Hilgris
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Venomous Snake.description: A very long snake, yellow, green, brown or black with pale bands, that can rear up a meter off the ground to face a threat.[1]
Giant Venomous Snake.lore:
The king cobra usually grows three to four meters long and can reach more than five.[1] It hunts by day and eats mostly other snakes, including rat snakes and pythons up to three meters long. Some king cobras eat only one kind of snake and refuse anything else.[1]

Its venom is a powerful nerve poison that can kill quickly by stopping breathing.[1] Even so, a king cobra usually tries to escape unless it is cornered. In a threat display it rears up about a meter and can follow its enemy while upright.[1]

Nesting females are the exception. A female piles plant matter into a nest where the heat of the rotting leaves keeps her eggs warm, and she may attack without warning.[1]

sources.title: Ophiophagus hannah (king cobra)
sources.author: Diana Young
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Vulture.description: A huge black vulture with a bare head, a white collar of down and white patches on wings spanning more than three meters.[1]
Giant Vulture.lore:
The Andean condor has the longest wingspan of any land bird, more than three meters, and can weigh up to 15 kilograms.[1] It lives high in the Andes of South America, nesting and roosting on cliff ledges and in caves, and it rides the warm air rising off the cliffs to soar for hours with hardly a wingbeat, scanning the ground for carrion.[1]

Condors find food by sight, while the smaller vultures that share their skies find it by smell. The two often feed together: the condor tears open the tough hide of a carcass, and the smaller vultures eat what it leaves.[1] Condors are thought to mate for life, and many may gather at a shared roost. Nearly two hundred have been seen together in Patagonia.[1]

sources.title: Vultur gryphus (Andean condor)
sources.author: Travis Kidd
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Wasp.description: The largest hornet in the world, with queens more than five centimeters long and a venomous sting.[1]
Giant Wasp.lore:
The Asian giant hornet is the largest hornet in the world.[1] It lives in colonies that nest underground, in holes it digs or takes over from small rodents, or in hollow trees.[1] Workers hunt beetles, mantises and caterpillars, and this is the only wasp known to stage group attacks on beehives and other wasps' nests. Twenty or thirty hornets can kill as many as 25,000 honeybees in a few hours.[1]

They mark a target hive with scent to call their nestmates to the attack, and they chew their prey into balls to carry home to their young.[1] When threatened they click their jaws as a warning before they sting. In Japan their stings kill an estimated 30 to 50 people a year.[1]

sources.title: Vespa mandarinia (Asian giant hornet)
sources.author: Zach Barth and Thomas Kearns
sources.publisher: Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology

Giant Weasel.description: A heavy, powerful member of the weasel family with short legs, broad clawed paws and a fierce temper.[1]
Giant Weasel.lore:
The wolverine is one of the largest members of the weasel family, weighing up to 30 kilograms.[1] It lives alone and guards its territory, marking it and its hidden food stores with a strong scent.[1]

It eats anything from eggs to moose. When deep snow leaves a deer or reindeer stranded, a wolverine can bring down prey five times its size, running over the snow on its broad, padded paws at more than 48 kilometers an hour.[1] It also scavenges, finding carrion with its keen nose.[1]

Wolverines are fierce enough to stand off wolves and mountain lions many times their size.[1] They raid trappers' lines and break into cabins and food stores, eating what they can and spraying the rest with their scent, and they can bite into cans with their sharp teeth.[1]

sources.title: Gulo gulo (wolverine)

Giant Wolf Spider.description: A big, hairy, dark gray spider with pale stripes down its back that hunts on the ground without a web.[1][2]
Giant Wolf Spider.lore:
Wolf spiders don't spin webs to catch food. They hunt. The rabid wolf spider, one of the most common spiders in the United States, sits motionless watching for movement, then overpowers its prey. It eats crickets, grasshoppers, ants and even other spiders, and it is not easily scared off by bigger animals.[1] The Hawaiian wolf spider has been seen climbing brush and leaping off to catch insects in midair.[2]

Wolf spiders look after their young. A female Hawaiian wolf spider carries her spiderlings on her back for several weeks after they hatch.[2] The rabid wolf spider has a fearsome name and a bite many people dread, but it is harmless to people.[1]

Goat.description: A sure-footed herd animal with hollow horns that sweep back or twist like corkscrews. Billy goats grow beards and carry a strong smell.[1]
Goat.lore:
Goats have lived with people for a very long time, and there are many breeds, from small to large.[1] People keep them for milk, cheese, meat, wool and leather, and more people around the world drink goat's milk and eat goat meat than rely on cattle for them.[1]

Goats are social and dislike being alone. Wild herds number from five to twenty, sometimes up to a hundred, and spend the day grazing.[1] Every herd has a pecking order, and the males settle theirs by butting heads.[1]

Coyotes, dogs, mountain lions, foxes, eagles and bobcats all hunt goats. A goat's best defense is its herd, but it will also fight back with its horns.[1]

Griffon.description: A fierce beast with the long ears and hooked beak of a bird of prey, said to guard great hoards of gold.[1][2]
Griffon.lore:
The Greeks heard of griffins from the far north. Herodotus wrote that a great store of gold lay in the north of Europe, and that the one-eyed Arimaspians stole it from the griffins that guarded it, though he doubted the tale himself.[1] The poet Aristeas, he says, placed the gold-guarding griffins beyond the land of the Arimaspians, and told of all these peoples forever at war with their neighbors.[1]

Pliny the Elder described griffins with long ears and hooked beaks, said to live in Ethiopia, and he counted them among fabulous creatures.[2]

Harpy.description: A winged woman, swift as the storm wind, who swoops down to snatch away food and leave the rest befouled.[1][2]
Harpy.lore:
The Harpies were daughters of Thaumas and Electra. Hesiod names them Aello, Storm-swift, and Ocypetes, Swift-flier, and says they kept pace with the winds and the birds.[1]

The gods sent them to torment the blind seer Phineus. Whenever a meal was laid before him they swooped down from the sky, snatched most of it away, and left the rest so foul that no one could touch it.[2] The winged sons of the North Wind, sailing with the Argonauts, chased them through the air. Some say the Harpies died in the chase, and others that they swore never to trouble Phineus again.[2]

Later tales give them a sweeter danger: a song that lures travelers close, after which their claws do the rest.

Hawk.description: A bird of prey with a wingspan over a meter, a brown back, a pale belly and powerful claws.[1]
Hawk.lore:
Red-tailed hawks hunt mostly from a perch, watching for prey and dropping onto it to kill with their powerful claws.[1] Most of what they eat are small rodents, along with rabbits, reptiles and other birds.[1] They also soar over their land on clear days, watching for intruders.[1]

A pair often stays together for years on the same territory and defends it hard. The female guards the nest, while the male drives intruders off the borders.[1] As with many birds of prey, the female is the larger of the two.[1]

Their cry is a harsh, screaming "kee-eeee-arrr", often compared to a steam whistle.[1]

Hell Hound.description: A fearsome hound of the underworld that guards the gates of the dead.[1][2]
Hell Hound.lore:
Cerberus was the hound of Hades, a child of Echidna and Typhaon. Hesiod calls him a monster not to be overcome, brazen-voiced, eating raw flesh, with fifty heads.[1] Apollodorus gives him three dog's heads, a dragon for a tail, and the heads of snakes along his back.[2]

Bringing him up from the underworld was the last labor of Heracles. Hades allowed it only if Heracles could master the dog without his weapons, so the hero wrapped his arms around its heads and held on, though the dragon in its tail bit him, until the beast gave in.[2]

Other hounds of the underworld are said to run in packs and to breathe fire.

Hill Giant.description: A huge, grim giant who lives in a cave and wades out to steal cattle, sheep and pigs from the farms around it.[1]
Hill Giant.lore:
In the days of King Arthur, the giant Cormoran lived in a cave on the Mount of Cornwall. He stood eighteen feet tall, with a fierce, grim face, and every town nearby lived in terror of him. When he was hungry he waded across to the mainland, and people fled their houses as he came. He carried off half a dozen oxen at once on his back and hung sheep and pigs from his belt.[1]

The magistrates promised the giant's treasure to whoever could kill him. A farmer's son named Jack crossed to the Mount one winter evening and dug a deep pit through the night and covered it with straw and earth. At dawn he blew a horn. The angry giant charged out of his cave, swearing to broil Jack for breakfast, and fell into the pit, where Jack killed him with a blow of his pickaxe. Jack was called the Giant-Killer from then on, and another giant, Blunderbore, swore revenge on him.[1]

Hippopotamus.description: A huge, barrel-shaped animal with thin purple-gray skin, short legs and a wide mouth armed with tusks.[1]
Hippopotamus.lore:
Hippos spend their days in rivers, lakes and swamps, resting in herds of 20 to 100 in water deep enough to cover them, often with their heads on each other's backs.[1] At dusk they come ashore and follow their own worn paths to graze, spending four or five hours a night pulling up grass with lips half a meter wide.[1]

They look clumsy but are not. A hippo can run at 30 kilometers an hour on land, and in shallow water it pushes along the bottom with its short, powerful legs.[1] Its skin oozes an oily red fluid, once thought to be blood mixed with sweat, which works as a sunscreen and keeps germs at bay.[1]

Hippos are loud. Their honking calls carry through the air and the water at the same time, the only mammal calls known to do so.[1] Bulls fight for rank by yawning to show their teeth, roaring, clashing jaws and tusks, and flinging dung with their swinging tails.[1] Apart from people, a grown hippo has no predators.[1]

Hunter Shark.description: A large, torpedo-shaped shark, dark gray above and white below, with broad, saw-edged triangular teeth.[1]
Hunter Shark.lore:
The great white shark is the best known of the big hunting sharks. It lives in temperate and subtropical seas around the world and sits at the top of the food chain.[1] It can grow to about six meters long and weigh more than 1,800 kilograms.[1] Young sharks eat fish, rays and squid. Larger ones gather around seal and sea lion colonies to hunt, and sometimes feed on dead whales.[1]

The white shark is partly warm-blooded. It keeps its body warmer than the water around it, which lets it hunt hard in cool seas.[1] It grows slowly and does not breed until it is about 26 to 33 years old, and estimates of its lifespan run from 30 to more than 70 years.[1]

Hydra.description: A huge serpent with nine heads that grows two new heads for every one cut off.[2]
Hydra.lore:
The Hydra of Lerna was a child of the monster Echidna, and the goddess Hera raised it out of anger at Heracles.[1] It lived in the swamp of Lerna and came out to ravage the cattle and the countryside. It had a huge body and nine heads, and eight of them could die, but the middle one was immortal.[2]

Killing it was the second labor of Heracles. He drove it out of its den with burning arrows and seized it, but it coiled around his foot, and each head he smashed grew back as two. A giant crab came to the Hydra's aid and bit his foot.[2]

His companion Iolaus burned the stumps of the necks with torches so no new heads could grow, and Heracles cut off the immortal head and buried it under a heavy rock beside the road. He slit open the body and dipped his arrows in its gall.[2]

Hyena.description: A strongly built, spotted hunter with a massive neck, rounded ears, a back that slopes down from the shoulders and some of the strongest jaws of any mammal.[1]
Hyena.lore:
Hyenas are known as scavengers, but the spotted hyena does most of its own killing. In one study, seven of every ten meals were animals it had hunted itself.[1] It hunts in small groups, or larger ones for zebra, and eats almost anything, from wildebeest and buffalo to ostrich eggs, porcupines and termites.[1]

Spotted hyenas live in clans of up to 80. Females rule: every female outranks every male, daughters stay in the clan for life, and males leave to join other clans, where they must wait their turn for rank.[1]

They are noisy. A whoop calls the clan together, a fast whoop rings out at a kill, and the famous giggle, the hyena's "laugh", comes from a hyena that is scared or excited, often while it is being chased.[1] Lions are their great rivals. The two often steal each other's kills, and their fights can end in death.[1]

Iron Golem.description: A giant made of metal, forged to stand guard without ever tiring.[1]
Iron Golem.lore:
Talos was a man of bronze who guarded the island of Crete. Some said he was the last of the Bronze Race of men, and others that the smith god Hephaestus made him and gave him to King Minos.[1] Three times a day he ran around the whole island, and when he saw the ship Argo coming close to shore, he pelted it with stones.[1]

A single vein ran from his neck to his ankles, sealed with a bronze nail. The sorceress Medea brought about his death, either by driving him mad with drugs or by promising to make him immortal and then pulling out the nail, so that the ichor poured out of him.[1]

Later makers built their guardians of iron. Such a golem fights with bladed arms and breathes poison, and fire only makes it stronger.

Jackal.description: A small wild dog with a pointed muzzle, tall pointed ears and a reddish-brown coat.[1]
Jackal.lore:
Jackals live almost anywhere, from open grassland and desert to the edges of towns.[1] They eat what they can get: insects, rodents, hares and small antelope, along with plants and scraps. They hunt alone, in pairs, or in packs when they go after bigger prey, and they wait at a lion's or leopard's kill to pick it over before the vultures finish it.[1]

Their ears and noses are sharp. A jackal on the hunt walks slowly with its ears pricked, and a startled jackal runs off, then circles back in a wide arc to catch the scent of whatever scared it.[1] Jackals are cunning and wary of people, and they turn aggressive only to defend their territory.[1]

Killer Whale.description: A large black-and-white whale with white patches by its eyes. Grown males carry a tall fin on their backs.[1]
Killer Whale.lore:
The killer whale, or orca, is the largest member of the dolphin family and the top predator in the sea. It lives in every ocean, in open water and along coasts.[1]

Orcas live in family groups called pods, built around mothers and their relatives, usually from a few to 20 or more whales, and most stay close to their family all their lives.[1] They talk with clicks, whistles and pulsed calls. Each population has its own calls, which the young learn from their elders, and the calls work like family badges.[1]

What an orca eats depends on what its group has learned to hunt. Off the northwest coast of North America, one kind eats almost nothing but salmon, while another, in the same waters, hunts seals and other sea mammals. They often hunt as a team.[1]

Lamia.description: A serpent with a woman's mouth and a woman's voice, who can take the shape of a lovely woman.[1]
Lamia.lore:
In John Keats's poem Lamia, the lamia is a serpent with brilliant, many-colored coils, a woman's mouth and eyes that weep at their own beauty. She was once a woman and longs to be one again.[1] She strikes a bargain with the god Hermes: she shows him the nymph he is searching for, and he gives her a woman's shape so she can go to Lycius, a young man of Corinth whom she loves.[1]

They live together in a hidden palace, until their wedding feast, when the old philosopher Apollonius stares at her and names her a serpent. With a scream she vanishes, and Lycius dies that same night.[1]

Other tales make the lamia a creature of the hells, a clawed fiend that leaps on its prey and whose touch corrupts.

Lion.description: A big, tawny cat with powerful forelegs. Adult males wear shaggy manes that range from blond to almost black.[1]
Lion.lore:
Lions are the most social of all cats. They live in prides of related females and their cubs, with one or more males, and a pride can number up to 40.[1] The females do most of the hunting, often closing in on prey from several directions before they charge, and they bring down animals as large as zebra and wildebeest.[1] Lions also steal kills from hyenas and leopards, and sometimes lose their own to groups of hyenas.[1]

Males guard the pride, and both males and females mark their land with scent and with roars that carry for about eight kilometers.[1] Young males are driven out at two to four years old. They band together with brothers and cousins and roam until they can take over a pride, and they usually hold it for about two years before another group drives them out.[1]

Wild lions now live only in Africa, apart from a small population in the Gir Forest of northwest India.[1]

Lizard.description: A small, quick reptile with scaly skin, four legs and a long tail, often seen basking on a sun-warmed rock.[1]
Lizard.lore:
Lizards are cold-blooded and take their heat from the sun, which costs them little and leaves more energy for hunting and raising young. They cannot pant or sweat, though, so in great heat they must find shade.[2] They hunt insects, spiders, scorpions and even other lizards, and in winter they tuck themselves away in dens until it warms up.[1][2]

A lizard bobbing up and down on a rock as if doing push-ups is defending its territory or courting a mate, and some show bright colors in the mating season.[1] Collared lizards can rise up and run on their hind legs to get away fast.[2]

Many lizards can drop their tails to escape a predator. The lost tail keeps wriggling to distract the attacker, and the lizard grows a new one, though that costs it a lot of energy.[1][2] Some kinds of whiptail lizard are all female and reproduce without males.[2]

Mammoth.description: An extinct elephant with long tusks that curve in a spiral, a domed head and a back that slopes down from high shoulders.[1]
Mammoth.lore:
Mammoths were elephants, close relatives of the elephants alive today. Their line began in Africa, and over millions of years mammoths spread across Europe and Asia and crossed a land bridge into North America.[1] Early mammoths ate leaves from shrubs and trees. Later ones grazed the cold, dry grasslands that once stretched across Asia.[1]

The best known is the woolly mammoth, with its thick, dark brown coat. Even woolly mammoths did not live in endless snow. They needed plenty of plants and kept mostly to places where the snow was not deep.[1]

Woolly mammoths were still thriving 20,000 years ago. Over the next 10,000 years they dwindled to small herds on islands off Siberia and Alaska, and about 4,000 years ago the last of them died.[2]

Manticore.description: A beast with a man's face and ears, a lion's body the color of blood and a tail ending in a sting.[1]
Manticore.lore:
Pliny the Elder, drawing on the Greek writer Ctesias, described the mantichora of Ethiopia. It had a triple row of teeth that fitted together like the teeth of a comb, the face and ears of a man, and blue eyes. Its body was a lion's, the color of blood, and its tail ended in a sting like a scorpion's.[1]

Its voice sounded like a flute and a trumpet together. It was astonishingly fast, and it was especially fond of human flesh.[1]

Later travelers' tales give it a tail bristling with spikes, which it can fling at its prey from a distance.

Mastiff.description: A large, powerful dog kept to guard people, homes and camps.[1][2]
Mastiff.lore:
Dogs were the first animals people tamed. They descend from wolves, and one idea is that wolves drawn to human camps by the smell of meat and scraps began to guard those camps from predators and to help with the hunt.[1] Over time, dogs came in every shape and size, from tiny Chihuahuas to huge Saint Bernards.[1]

Big dogs have long stood guard for soldiers too. On Guam in 1944, war dogs served as sentries and scouts. They sniffed out snipers and hidden mines, warned of ambushes and guarded camps at night, and Marines said they slept better knowing the dogs were watching.[2]

Medusa.description: A woman whose hair is a mass of living snakes and whose gaze turns anyone who meets it to stone.[2]
Medusa.lore:
Medusa was one of the three Gorgons, sisters who lived beyond the ocean at the edge of the world, toward the land of night. Her sisters Stheno and Euryale could neither die nor grow old, but Medusa was mortal.[1]

Ovid tells that she was once a famous beauty, admired above all for her hair, until the god of the sea assaulted her in the temple of Minerva. The goddess punished Medusa by turning that hair into hideous snakes.[2] Around her lair stood men and beasts turned to stone by the sight of her.[2]

The hero Perseus found her by stealing the single eye shared by the two Gray Sisters. He looked at her only in the reflection of his bronze shield, and while Medusa and her snakes slept, he cut off her head.[2] From her neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus and the giant Chrysaor.[1][2] As Perseus flew home over the deserts of Libya, drops of her blood fell to the ground and became snakes, which is why, Ovid says, that land is full of them.[2]

Merfolk.description: A being of the sea, human in shape above, with a body rough with scales.[1]
Merfolk.lore:
Pliny the Elder collected reports of the people of the sea. A delegation from Olisipo told the emperor Tiberius that a triton had been seen and heard in a cave, blowing a conch shell, and looking just as tritons are usually shown.[1]

Nereids were real too, Pliny wrote, though the human part of their bodies was rough all over with scales. One was seen dying on that same shore, and people far away heard its mournful cries, and a governor of Gaul wrote to the emperor Augustus that many nereids had been found dead on the beach.[1] Men of rank told Pliny they had seen a sea-man off Gades, human in every part, who climbed onto ships at night and weighed them down until they nearly sank.[1]

Minotaur of Baphomet.description: A huge man with the head of a bull.[1]
Minotaur of Baphomet.lore:
When King Minos of Crete failed to sacrifice a bull to Poseidon, the god made the animal savage and filled the queen, Pasiphae, with desire for it. She bore the Minotaur, named Asterius, who had a bull's face on a man's body. Minos shut him away in the Labyrinth, a maze of winding passages built by the craftsman Daedalus.[1]

Athens had to send people to Crete as tribute to the Minotaur, and the hero Theseus went with the third tribute. Ariadne, the daughter of Minos, fell in love with him, and on Daedalus's advice she gave him a ball of thread. Theseus tied it to the door and unwound it as he went in, found the Minotaur in the farthest part of the maze and killed it with his fists, then followed the thread back out.[2]

Other tales tell of whole tribes of bull-headed warriors who charge with lowered horns and fight with great glaives.

Mule.description: A sturdy cross between a horse and a donkey, with long ears, small hooves and great endurance.[1]
Mule.lore:
A mule is the offspring of a female horse and a male donkey. From the donkey it gets intelligence, long ears and small, sure-footed hooves, and from the horse a willing nature, endurance and strength.[1] George Washington bred mules at Mount Vernon from his best mares.[1]

In the 1800s mules were the "engines" of the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal, towing boats loaded with goods and people, and two to three thousand worked the canal each year.[1][2] Boat captains preferred them to horses. Mules cost less, fell sick and got hurt less often, had tougher skin and were less likely to stumble.[2] A team of two or three mules could tow a 140-ton boat for about eight hours, then rest in a stable on the boat while another team took over.[2] Canal workers named their mules and often treated them like pets.[2]

Octopus.description: A soft-bodied sea animal with eight sucker-lined arms and no shell, able to change its color and shape to vanish against the seabed.[1]
Octopus.lore:
Octopuses are clever. They learn, and they can tell things apart by sight, touch and taste.[1] The common octopus keeps a hidden home in a hole or crack in the rocks, and it often blocks the entrance with shells and stones it has gathered.[1]

Few animals hide as well. An octopus can change its color, its skin texture and its posture to blend in with almost any surface.[1] It hunts snails and clams.[1] Newly hatched octopuses drift and hunt among the plankton for weeks before they settle on the sea floor.[1]

Ogre.description: A huge, cruel brute who eats people, especially children, and is often richer and stronger than it is clever.[1]
Ogre.lore:
Charles Perrault's tales are full of ogres. In Little Thumb, seven lost brothers take shelter in an ogre's house, though his wife warns them that he eats little children.[1] The ogre smells them hiding under the bed and decides to kill them in the morning. In the night, the youngest boy swaps his brothers' caps for the gold crowns worn by the ogre's seven daughters. The ogre comes in the dark with his great knife, feels for the crowns and kills his own daughters instead.[1] He chases the boys in boots that cover seven leagues at a stride, but the effort tires him and he falls asleep, and the boy steals the boots from his feet.[1]

In Puss in Boots, the richest ogre ever known could turn himself into any animal he liked. The clever cat asked to see him become a lion, then a mouse, and when the ogre did, the cat ate him.[1]

Other tales make the ogre a hulking, dim-witted giant who smashes enemies with a great club and hurls javelins.

Owl.description: A big owl with tufts of feathers like horns, a round face, forward-facing eyes and a white patch at the throat.[1]
Owl.lore:
Great horned owls hunt at night and find their way and their prey in the dark, even in thick forest.[1] They watch from a perch, then swoop down, catching prey on the wing if they have to, and they screech loudly as they strike.[1] They eat rabbits, voles and other rodents, and near water they catch fish, frogs, crabs and reptiles.[1]

These owls live alone except when nesting, and they stay in the same area all year.[1] Their deep "hoo-hoo hoooo hoo-hoo" marks their territory and can be heard for kilometers, and fights over territory can be deadly.[1] Some owls have no territory of their own and wander through the lands of others.[1]
