Panther.description: A sleek, powerful big cat that hunts by stealth. Depending on where it lives, its coat may be spotted, plain tawny or solid black.[1][2]
Panther.lore:
Panther is a name given to more than one big cat. A black panther is a leopard born with black fur, most often in humid forests.[1] In Florida, the panther is the local puma, a long-tailed cat with plain brown or rusty fur.[2]

The leopard hunts alone, mostly at night. It creeps low until it is a few meters from its prey, then pounces, and if the pounce misses it rarely gives chase.[1] It can take prey up to ten times its own weight, and it often carries the kill up into a tree to eat in peace.[1]

Leopards are at home in trees and climb down head first. They mark their land with scent and claw marks, and they announce themselves with a hoarse, rasping cough repeated again and again.[1]

Pegasus.description: A winged horse that sprang from the neck of the Gorgon Medusa when the hero Perseus cut off her head.[1]
Pegasus.lore:
Pegasus was born when Perseus beheaded Medusa. Hesiod says his name comes from the springs of the Ocean, near which he was born.[1] He left the earth for the home of the gods, and he lives in the house of Zeus and carries the god's thunder and lightning.[1]

Before that, he carried the hero Bellerophon, flying tirelessly over land and sea as fast as the wind, and together they killed the fire-breathing Chimera.[1]

Where his hoof struck Mount Helicon, the home of the Muses, a new spring burst from the rock, the spring called Hippocrene, and the goddess Minerva came to see it.[2]

Piranha.description: A river fish with a silver-gray back, a reddish-orange belly and black and reddish-orange fins.[1]
Piranha.lore:
The red-bellied piranha lives in the rivers of South America east of the Andes, including the Amazon and the Paraná-Paraguay.[1] Groups of 20 to 30 lie in wait among water plants and ambush prey that comes near. They also chase prey down and scavenge.[1] Small piranhas hunt by day, while the larger ones feed at dawn and in the late afternoon and evening.[1]

They eat whole fish and pieces of fish, fins, scales, insects, snails and plants.[1] The red-bellied piranha is counted among the more dangerous and aggressive piranhas, and it has bitten people.[1]

Plesiosaurus.description: A sea reptile with a long neck, a small head and four wing-shaped flippers that drove it through the water.[1]
Plesiosaurus.lore:
Plesiosaurs were reptiles of the open sea that lived while dinosaurs ruled the land, though they were only distant relatives of the dinosaurs.[1] Plesiosaurus itself was about 3.5 meters long and ate small prey such as fish and crustaceans. Its relatives grew as long as 12 meters, and some had necks longer than their bodies.[1][2]

They swam with four flippers, timing the strokes of the front and back pairs for extra push, and they could not come ashore, so they gave birth to live young at sea.[1] They swallowed stones, which may have helped them break up food or stay steady in the water. Their long necks were stiffer than a swan's and may have helped them sneak up on prey.[1]

Plesiosaurs lasted more than 140 million years and died out with the dinosaurs.[1][2] Mary Anning found the first nearly complete Plesiosaurus skeleton on the south coast of England in 1823, and plesiosaurs later inspired the legend of the Loch Ness Monster.[1]

Polar Bear.description: The great white bear of the Arctic sea ice, with a long neck, a small head, broad forepaws that work as paddles and fur on the soles of its feet.[1]
Polar Bear.lore:
Polar bears are the largest bears alive, and they live on the sea ice around the North Pole more than on land.[1][2] Seals are their main prey, especially ringed seals, and they also take walruses, belugas, seabirds and their eggs, and fish, or feed on dead whales.[1][2] A bear often eats only the fat of a kill and leaves the rest, and younger bears and Arctic foxes live off those leftovers.[1]

Most of a polar bear's time goes to resting or waiting still for prey, and much of the rest to walking and swimming. They are strong swimmers and range far in search of food.[1] Their fur looks white, but each hair is clear, and the skin underneath is black.[1]

Polar bears live alone, except for mothers with cubs. Black and brown bears den up through the winter, but among polar bears only pregnant females spend the winter in dens.[2] A mother will charge a much larger male to protect her cubs.[1]

Pony.description: A sturdy, hardy horse, tough enough to live on poor food through heat and storms.[1]
Pony.lore:
The wild ponies of Assateague Island, off the coast of Maryland and Virginia, are really feral horses, descended from domestic stock. They are probably the descendants of horses that mainland owners left on the island in the late 1600s to avoid fencing laws and livestock taxes, though local legend says they came ashore from a shipwreck.[1]

They live in bands of two to twelve, each with its own range, and they survive scorching heat, storms, swarms of mosquitoes and poor food. On buggy days they go down to the beach to escape the flies.[1] Every July the Virginia herd is swum across to Chincoteague Island for Pony Penning, and most of the young foals are sold at auction, a festival made famous by the book Misty of Chincoteague.[1]

Pteranodon.description: A large flying reptile with wings of skin stretched from one long finger to its ankles, and a long, toothless beak.[1]
Pteranodon.lore:
Pteranodon was a pterosaur, one of the flying reptiles. Pterosaurs are often called flying dinosaurs, but they were a group of reptiles of their own.[1] Each wing was a thin sheet of skin held up by one hugely long finger and reaching back to the ankle, while the other fingers stayed free as a hand.[1]

Pteranodon had no teeth, yet its fossils have been found with fish in their stomachs. It probably swooped down to the water and snatched fish from the surface, as some seabirds do.[1][2] Large pterosaurs may have flown like albatrosses, riding air currents over long distances and flapping only now and then.[1]

Rat.description: A large, coarse-furred rodent with bald ears and a long, bald tail.[1]
Rat.lore:
Wherever people go, rats follow. The brown rat started out in the forests of Asia and now lives in nearly every port city in the world, in sewers, dumps, basements and fields.[1] It eats almost anything, especially what people throw away, and it also takes chicks, mice, birds and lizards. Rats by the sea have been seen catching fish with their paws.[1]

Rats come out at dusk and at night to dig burrows, forage and build nests. They swim well and learn quickly, remembering their way through tangled sewers and tunnels.[1] Smell is their sharpest sense, and they can feel their way through total darkness with their whiskers and paws.[1]

Few animals have done people more harm. Rat fleas and lice carry plague, typhus and other diseases, and rat-borne disease is thought to have killed more people in the last thousand years than all wars together.[1]

Raven.description: A large, all-black bird with a heavy beak, a wedge-shaped tail and shaggy feathers at its throat.[1]
Raven.lore:
Ravens are the largest of the songbirds and among the cleverest of birds, able to work out new answers to problems they have never met.[1] They are mostly scavengers, drawn to carrion, but they eat almost anything: insects, frogs, small mammals, birds, grain, acorns and fruit.[1]

They are talkers. Scientists have counted between 15 and 33 kinds of calls, from alarms to chase calls to calls that claim territory, and the shaggy throat feathers play a part in how ravens deal with each other.[1] Most ravens live alone or in pairs, but they gather where food is plentiful, and young birds roost together.[1] Ravens soar and glide more than most crows, and their harsh croak gives them away.[1]

Reef Shark.description: A slender gray shark with a white belly, white tips on its fins and a short, broad snout.[1]
Reef Shark.lore:
Reef sharks live around tropical coral reefs, and each kind keeps to its own part of the reef. The blacktip reef shark keeps to the shallow coastal water, and the gray reef shark to the deep water off the reef edge.[1]

By day the whitetip reef shark rests in caves and deep cracks in the reef, often lying still on the bottom, which it can do because it pumps water over its gills without swimming. It returns to the same cave day after day for months.[1]

At night it changes. It becomes an aggressive hunter, thrashing through the reef for fish, sometimes together with other sharks, and it will wedge half its body into a crack to reach a fish hiding inside.[1] Whitetips are calm around divers but will fight spear fishers over a speared fish.[1]

Rhinoceros.description: A massive, short-legged beast with thick, wrinkled skin like riveted armor and one or two solid horns on its snout.[1]
Rhinoceros.lore:
There are five kinds of rhinoceros: three in south-central Asia and two in Africa south of the Sahara. They live in grassland, scrub and dense forest, never far from water they can reach each day.[1] Their horns are not bone but solid, packed keratin.[1]

The black rhino of Africa mostly keeps to itself. It feeds in the morning and evening and rests through the heat of the day, rolling in mud to stay cool.[2] It browses on twigs, shrubs and small trees, gripping them with its grasping upper lip, and knocks branches down with its horn to reach higher ones.[2]

Black rhinos see poorly, only 25 to 30 meters, and rely on their noses.[2] A startled black rhino runs off snorting, then often turns back out of curiosity and charges whatever scared it. These charges look dangerous but rarely end badly.[2] Rhinos leave their dung in shared piles, which tells other rhinos who has passed and how recently.[2]

Riding Horse.description: A quick horse with long, slender legs, a long neck, a flowing mane and a long tail, bred to carry a rider.[1]
Riding Horse.lore:
Horses are herd animals. In the wild they live in bands, usually several mares and one or more stallions with their young, and every band has its own order of rank.[1]

They rely mostly on their eyes, and their long, upright ears catch sounds. Whiskers on the muzzle and cheeks let them feel what is close.[1] People have depended on horses for a very long time: to carry riders and goods, to pull plows and carriages, in war and in sport.[1]

Saber-Toothed Tiger.description: A powerful cat with strong forelegs and two upper fangs up to 28 centimeters long.[1]
Saber-Toothed Tiger.lore:
The saber-toothed tiger, Smilodon, lived in the Americas from about 2.5 million years ago until about 12,000 years ago.[1] It killed with its long fangs, gripping prey with its powerful forelegs and driving the teeth home with a head movement of its own.[1] Saber-toothed hunters may have been able to bring down fully grown large animals, perhaps by striking at the blood vessels of the neck.[1]

Long fangs like these evolved many times, in animals as different as a South American marsupial and the false saber-toothed cats, but Smilodon is the most famous saber-tooth of all.[1]

For all its fangs, its nose was weak. Scans of its skull suggest its sense of smell was poorer than a house cat's or a wolf's, no better than a mouse's.[2]

Satyr.description: A wild man of the woods with red hair and a tail almost as large as a horse's.[1]
Satyr.lore:
Satyrs are wild spirits of the countryside, and the old ones were called Sileni.[1] The traveler Pausanias heard from a sailor named Euphemus about the Satyr-islands, far out in a sea where ships no longer sailed. Their people were red-haired, with tails at their loins nearly as large as a horse's. They ran down to the ship without a word and laid hands on the women aboard, and the frightened sailors had to put to sea again.[1]

The satyr Marsyas once challenged the god Apollo to a contest of music, playing the flute. He lost, and Apollo flayed him alive for his pride. The fauns, the nymphs and his brother satyrs wept for him, and their tears became a river that bears his name.[2]

Scorpion.description: A small, eight-legged hunter with grasping pincers and a long tail tipped with a venomous stinger.[1][2]
Scorpion.lore:
Scorpions are close relatives of spiders. All of them carry venom, and they come out at night to hunt, using the stinger to kill prey or to defend themselves.[2] The bark scorpion of the American Southwest grabs insects with its pincers and stings them with its highly venomous tail.[1]

Under ultraviolet light scorpions glow, which makes them easy to find at night.[1][2] A female bark scorpion gives birth to live young and carries as many as 30 on her back for up to three weeks, until they shed their first skin.[1]

A venomous sting doesn't always save a scorpion. Bats, mice, lizards, tarantulas and birds all eat bark scorpions.[1]

Seahorse.description: A small fish with a horse-like head set at a right angle to its body and a body armored with bony rings.[1]
Seahorse.lore:
Seahorses spend most of their lives in a small patch of seagrass or coral, holding on and watching for food.[1] They hunt by sight, mostly by day, and when a small shrimp or fish comes close they suck it into their snouts.[1] Some can change color to hide or to court a mate.[1]

Seahorse pairs often stay together season after season. The female passes her eggs to the male, who carries them in a pouch until they hatch.[1] Some seahorses travel far by clinging to floating mats of seaweed.[1] They are small, and many animals eat them, from fish, turtles and seabirds to crabs and shrimp.[1]

Sphinxes.description: A winged lion with the face of a woman, who asks riddles and devours those who cannot answer.[2]
Sphinxes.lore:
Hesiod names the Sphinx as a child of Echidna and the destroyer of the people of Thebes.[1] Apollodorus says the goddess Hera sent her. She had a woman's face, a lion's chest, feet and tail, and a bird's wings. She sat on a mountain above Thebes and asked the riddle she had learned from the Muses: what has one voice, yet goes on four feet, then two, then three? Whenever the Thebans failed to answer, she snatched one of them and ate him.[2]

Oedipus solved it. A man crawls on all fours as a baby, walks on two feet as an adult, and leans on a staff in old age. The Sphinx threw herself from the citadel.[2] In Egypt, Herodotus saw great statues of sphinxes with the heads of men.[3]

Other tales tell of sphinxes as wise guardians sent by the gods, keepers of secret knowledge whose roar can shake the mind.

Spider.description: An eight-legged hunter with fangs and venom that spins silk, sometimes into great wheel-shaped webs.[1][2]
Spider.lore:
All spiders make silk, the strongest natural material known, but not all of them spin webs. Some stalk their prey or ambush it from hiding. Spiders also use silk for signal lines, nurseries and egg cases, and baby spiders float on silk threads to travel long distances on the wind.[1]

Spiders can't eat solid food. They use venom and digestive juices to turn their prey to liquid, then suck it up.[1] Every spider has fangs and venom, but most can't hurt people, because their venom is too weak or their fangs too small to break the skin.[1]

The golden silk spider of the southeastern United States spins a round web up to a meter across, held up by strong, non-sticky yellow strands and filled with very sticky ones.[2] The female is many times the size of the male, and after mating she kills and eats him, using the meal to make her eggs.[2]

Stone Giant.description: A giant with a heart and head of stone, who fights behind a thick stone shield and hurls great stones.[1]
Stone Giant.lore:
Hrungnir was the strongest of the giants. His heart was made of stone, sharp and three-cornered, and his head was stone too. He carried a broad, thick shield of stone, and his weapon was a huge flint-stone that he swung over his shoulder.[1]

After a drunken visit to the halls of the gods, he challenged Thor to a duel at the borders of the giants' land. The giants built him a huge companion out of clay, but it was so terrified at the sight of Thor that it wet itself.[1] Hrungnir was tricked into standing on his shield, and when Thor hurled his hammer, Hrungnir threw his flint-stone to meet it. The stone shattered in the air. Its pieces became the flint in the mountains, and one shard struck Thor's head and stuck fast there. The hammer crushed the giant's skull, and he fell with his foot across Thor's neck, so heavy that none of the gods could lift it.[1]

Storm Giant.description: A giant who sits at the edge of the sky, wrapped in an eagle's feathers, and raises the wind with his wings.[1]
Storm Giant.lore:
The wind is strong enough to stir up great seas and fan fires to flame, yet no one can see it. The Prose Edda explains where it comes from. At the northern end of heaven sits a giant named Hrasvelg, dressed in the shape of an eagle. Whenever he spreads his wings to fly, the winds rise from under them and blow over all the world.[1]

Other tales tell of storm giants who live beneath the sea as easily as on land, hurl thunderbolts and call down storms of lightning. These giants are often kind, if rarely gentle.

sources.title: The Younger Edda, Also Called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda

Swarm of Bats.description: Hundreds of bats that roost together by day in caves, mines and hollow trees, then fill the night air as they hunt by sound.[1][2]
Swarm of Bats.lore:
Bats spend the day out of sight, packed into caves, old mines, hollow trees and cracks in rock, or under bridges, where predators can't reach them. Some of these places fill with bats each spring as mothers gather to raise their young, and others fill each winter as bats crowd in to sleep through the cold.[1] On summer evenings, many come out to hunt insects over ponds and streams.[1]

Bats find their way and their prey in the dark by calling out and listening for the echoes, at a pitch too high for people to hear. When a bat closes in on an insect, its calls speed up into a fast buzz just before it strikes.[2]

Not every bat hunts insects. Some eat fruit or pollen, and a few even catch fish.[3]

Swarm of Insects.description: A mass of insects rising together in a cloud.[1]
Swarm of Insects.lore:
Insects outnumber every other kind of animal. Around 90,000 kinds have been described in the United States and Canada alone, and there may be tens of millions of species of insects and their relatives worldwide.[2] Every insect has six legs and a body in three parts: head, thorax and abdomen.[2]

Some insects appear in vast numbers all at once. Mayflies spend up to a year as young in the water, under rocks and rotting plants, then emerge together in huge numbers to breed, and a winged adult may live only a couple of hours.[1] Grasshoppers, also called locusts, fill meadows with their "singing", made by snapping their wings in flight or rubbing their legs against their wings.[1]

Swarm of Piranhas.description: A school of twenty or more piranhas, each with interlocking, razor-sharp triangular teeth hidden behind thick lips.[1]
Swarm of Piranhas.lore:
Red-bellied piranhas travel in schools of 20 or more through the rivers of the Amazon basin.[1] Their jaws are short and powerful, with triangular teeth that lock together like shears. Yet in the wild much of what they eat is fins nipped from the tails of larger fish, along with bits of flesh, small fish, insects and ripe fruit.[1]

Their fearsome name comes largely from Theodore Roosevelt, who wrote of watching piranhas tear apart a cow in South America. In fact the fish had been netted and starved first, which drove them into a frenzy when the cow was pushed into the water.[2] Piranhas usually attack like that only when they are very hungry or defending their nests.[2]

Swarm of Rats.description: A crowd of rats with big ears and tails longer than their bodies.[1]
Swarm of Rats.lore:
The black rat, also called the ship rat or roof rat, came from India and has been carried by people to every continent. It thrives in ports and on ships, which is why it is most common along coasts.[1] It climbs well and nests high up, in the top floors of buildings or in trees.[1]

Black rats live in groups of several males and females, and they come out mostly at night.[1] They eat grain, fruit and other plants, and insects when they must, and they spoil far more food than they eat by fouling what they leave behind.[1]

The black rat is best known for its part in spreading the bubonic plague, which killed millions in the Middle Ages. Its fleas carry many diseases that can harm people and animals.[1]

Swarm of Ravens.description: A noisy flock of big, glossy black birds with heavy bills and wings spanning more than a meter.[1]
Swarm of Ravens.lore:
Ravens are social birds and sometimes gather in flocks of up to a hundred.[1] They have a wide range of calls, from the yell of a hungry nestling to the sharp keck-keck-keck alarm given when a hawk flies over, which may let them share a great deal of information.[1]

They are clever and quick to take advantage of people. Ravens have been seen playing with sticks and passing stones to each other, and in the California deserts their numbers have soared where people leave food behind.[1] In Yellowstone, some have learned to unzip and unsnap packs.[2]

Ravens follow wolves on the hunt to feed at their kills, since they cannot tear open thick hides on their own.[2] Native American stories have long told of the raven as a mischievous, clever animal.[1]

Swarm of Venomous Snakes.description: A tangle of rattlesnakes gathered together in a rocky den, rattles buzzing.[1][2]
Swarm of Venomous Snakes.lore:
Rattlesnakes spend the winter together. They gather in dens that reach below the frost line, sometimes in large groups and sometimes alongside other kinds of snakes, and they return to the same den year after year.[1] In some places the dens are in rock outcrops that face the sun.[2]

In spring they come out to bask, and most then spread out to hunt mice, rats, ground squirrels, birds and lizards. Pregnant females stay near the den, basking often, and give birth to live young in September.[2] By late September the snakes have gathered back at the den, and they crawl underground for another winter.[2]

Cornered, a rattlesnake coils and rattles a warning, but it does not always rattle before it strikes.[1]

Tiger.description: A huge cat with a reddish-orange coat, bold black stripes and a white belly. No two tigers have the same stripes.[1]
Tiger.lore:
Tigers hunt alone, mostly at night. A tiger lies in wait where its stripes hide it, then pounces, drags its prey to the ground and kills it with a bite to the neck.[1] Deer and wild boar are its main prey, but tigers also take monkeys, buffalo, bears, leopards and even crocodiles. They swim well and have been seen hunting in water.[1] A tiger hunts about once a week and can eat as much as 34 kilograms in a night.[1]

Tigers guard their land fiercely. They mark it with scent and claw marks on trees, and they roar, grunt and chuff to keep track of each other.[1] Cubs stay with their mother until they can hunt for themselves and leave at two or three years old to find land of their own.[1]

Tigers once lived across much of Asia, from the lands around the Caspian Sea to eastern Asia. They now hold only a small part of that range, in South and Southeast Asia, China and the Russian Far East.[1]

sources.title: Tiger
sources.publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute

Triceratops.description: A four-legged plant-eater with three horns, a parrot-like beak and a wide frill of bone behind its head.[1]
Triceratops.lore:
Triceratops had one of the largest skulls of any land animal, with a frill nearly a meter across.[1] It snipped plants with its sharp beak and ground them with rows of teeth at the back of its jaws, and it may have used its horns and frill to push through thick growth.[1]

Its horns were weapons. One fossil horn was bitten off by a Tyrannosaurus and then healed, so at least some Triceratops survived those fights. Males also seem to have fought each other with their horns.[1] In life the horns were covered in keratin, which made them longer and sharper than the fossil bone suggests.[1]

Many horned dinosaurs lived in herds, but Triceratops fossils are usually found alone, so it may have spent much of its life by itself.[1] Its skin was covered in large, pebbled scales.[1]

Troll.description: A huge, ugly man-eater of the forests and fells, with eyes as big as saucers, who hoards gold in its rocky home.[1]
Troll.lore:
In the folk tales of Norway, trolls live in the pine forests on the mountainsides and in caves deep inside the rock, where they sit among heaps of gold and silver. They carry off human children, and they eat people as readily as porridge or sausages, because that is their nature.[1] By day they keep to forests too dark for the sun to reach, and at night they come home, eat their fill and snore until morning.[1]

The sun is their bane. A troll that looks the sun full in the face bursts. In one tale, the Man o' the Hill is running home to his trapdoor at dawn when the sun rises, and he bursts on the spot. His gold is said to lie under the trapdoor still.[1] In another, a great ugly troll lives under a bridge over a stream and threatens to gobble up the three billy goats Gruff as they cross. The biggest goat charges him, crushes him to bits and tosses him into the stream.[1]

Other tales tell of trolls that no wound can stop. Cut one apart and its flesh knits back together, and a severed limb keeps fighting on its own. Only fire or acid keeps it from healing.

sources.title: Popular Tales from the Norse
sources.author: Peter Christen Asbjørnsen and Jørgen Moe, translated by Sir George Webbe Dasent

Tyrannosaurus Rex.description: A two-legged predator about 12 meters long, with a massive skull, small arms and saw-edged teeth strong enough to crush bone.[1]
Tyrannosaurus Rex.lore:
Tyrannosaurus rex lived at the very end of the age of dinosaurs. Its name means "tyrant lizard king".[1] Its jaws held 60 saw-edged teeth and gave it the strongest bite of any land animal known, strong enough to crush bone. It swallowed the pieces, too: bone turns up in its fossilized dung.[1]

It had a keen nose. Much of its brain was given over to smell, which let it follow living prey or find a carcass from far away.[1] Its tooth marks have been found on the bones of Triceratops and Edmontosaurus, and on the bones of other tyrannosaurs, so they fought each other too.[1]

Its arms were tiny for its size, and no one is sure what they were for. They may have helped it get back up after a fall, or held food while it was young.[1] Fossil skin shows it was covered in scales.[1]

Unicorn.description: A fierce, swift beast with a horse's body and a single long horn growing from the middle of its forehead.[1]
Unicorn.lore:
Ancient writers placed the one-horned beast in India. Pliny the Elder called it the monoceros, the "one-horn", and described it as very fierce, with the head of a stag, the feet of an elephant, the tail of a boar and the body of a horse.[1] It gave a deep lowing cry, and from the middle of its forehead grew a single black horn two cubits long.[1] It could not, he said, be taken alive.[1]

Later stories remember a gentler animal than Pliny's fierce monoceros: a creature of the heavens whose horn shines with holy light, which drives off evil and can heal those it chooses to bless.

Venomous Snake.description: A heavy-bodied snake with a broad, diamond-shaped head, slit pupils and a rattle at the tip of its tail.[1]
Venomous Snake.lore:
Venomous snakes make venom in glands in their heads and deliver it through a bite with needle-like fangs. Vipers and cobras inject it through hollow teeth.[2] Snakes first evolved venom to hunt, and some use it in defense as well.[2]

The rattlesnake is a pit viper. Its long, curved fangs fold back against the roof of its mouth and swing forward when it strikes, and it controls how much venom it injects.[1] Heat-sensing pits between its eyes and nostrils help it find warm-blooded prey, and its flicking tongue carries scent to an organ in the roof of its mouth.[1][2]

A rattlesnake's rattle is made of the segments left each time it sheds its skin. Shaken by the muscles at the base of the tail, the segments buzz against each other as a warning, though a rattlesnake does not always rattle before it strikes.[1]

Vulture.description: A big, brownish-black bird with a bare head and neck that feeds on carrion.[1]
Vulture.lore:
Vultures eat the dead. The turkey vulture finds carcasses by smell as well as sight, which makes it one of the few birds in the world that relies heavily on its nose, and black vultures follow it to its finds.[1] It eats roadkill, dead livestock and wild carrion, and it prefers fresh carcasses.[1]

Turkey vultures roost together, sometimes several hundred to a roost, but each searches for food alone by day.[1] They have little in the way of a voice: mostly grunts, hisses and barks to warn off predators.[1] Those in colder lands fly south for the winter.[1]

Warhorse.description: A strong, steady horse trained to carry a rider into battle.[2]
Warhorse.lore:
Armies once ran on horses. Some three million horses and mules served in the American Civil War, and about half of them died.[1] They pulled cannons and supply wagons and carried the wounded and the cavalry, and a battery of six guns needed 120 horses.[1] Few died from enemy fire. Most were worked to death or died of disease, often short of proper food, and a cavalry horse needed more than five times as much food each day as the soldier who rode it.[1]

A cavalry trooper's horse could decide whether a mission succeeded, and a trooper would nearly always see to his horse before himself.[2] In the 7th Cavalry, each company rode horses of a single color.[2] At the Little Bighorn, all the horses of the five companies that rode with Custer died except one, Comanche, who was wounded several times and survived.[2]

Weasel.description: A tiny, long, slender hunter with short legs, round ears and dark eyes. In the far north its brown coat turns pure white for winter.[1]
Weasel.lore:
The least weasel is the smallest meat-eater in the world, yet weasels are known for killing prey much bigger than themselves and hiding what they don't eat.[1] It lives almost entirely on mice and voles, and it hunts them by smell, following them into their tunnels underground.[1]

Weasels live alone, and the males are bullies: a dominant male threatens and viciously attacks lesser males, which run off squealing.[1] Weasels bark, hiss, chirp, squeal and trill.[1]

Owls, hawks, eagles and larger weasels all hunt them. A weasel defends itself by blending in or by screeching and biting.[1]

Wight.description: One of the restless dead, who guards its treasure in a dark burial mound and fights anyone who breaks in.[1]
Wight.lore:
In the saga of Grettir the Strong, a flame burned at night above a burial mound on Haramsey, an island off the coast of Norway. It belonged to Karr the Old, who had been buried there and had since haunted the island so badly that every other landowner had been driven away.[1] Grettir dug into the mound. Inside, in the dark and the stench, he found horse bones and a dead man sitting in a high chair over heaps of gold and silver. As he carried the treasure out, the barrow-dweller seized him, and they wrestled in the dark until the dead man fell. Grettir cut off his head and laid it at his thigh, the old way to keep a ghost from walking.[1]

The shepherd Glam was harder to put down. After his death he would not lie quiet. He rode the house roofs at night until they nearly broke, and people who saw him fainted or lost their minds. When Grettir finally threw him down, Glam's eyes glared up in the moonlight, and he cursed Grettir to see those eyes forever and to dread being alone.[1]

Other tales arm the wight with sword and bow and give it a touch that drains the life from the living. Sunlight weakens it.

sources.title: The Story of Grettir the Strong

Wolf.description: A lean wild dog with a coat anywhere from gray to brown, black or white, that hunts in family packs able to kill a moose or a bison.[1]
Wolf.lore:
Wolves live and hunt as families. A pack is usually a mated pair and their young, and the parents lead the hunts and teach the young how to hunt, avoid danger and mark the borders of their land.[1] Together they bring down caribou, moose and bison, animals far bigger than any one wolf, and they take rabbits, beavers, fish and even berries when they can.[1]

A pack's land can be huge, and wolves cover long distances across it, mostly at night.[2] They howl to call the pack together, to stir it up before a hunt and to warn other packs away. A wolf cut off from its pack gives a short, rising "lonesome howl", then switches to deeper calls once the others answer, so they can find it.[1]

Around two years of age, a young wolf may wander the edges of its family's land before leaving to find a mate and start a pack of its own.[1] Folklore has long cast wolves as animals to fear, and that fear still shapes how people treat them.[1]

Worg.description: A huge, evil wolf, one of a race of giants born in wolf shape in a dark forest at the edge of the world.[1]
Worg.lore:
The sun and moon race across the sky because wolves are chasing them. Skoll runs after the sun and will one day catch her, and Hati runs ahead trying to seize the moon.[1] East of the world of men lies the forest of Ironwood, where an old hag gives birth to many giant sons, all in the shape of wolves. The mightiest of this wolf race is Moongarm, who feeds on the blood of the dead. One day he will swallow the moon and stain the sky with blood, and the sun will go dark.[1]

Other tales describe worgs as cunning, evil wolves of the fey that speak their own language and the language of goblins.
